lessons.title: Collecting like terms
lessons.summary: Recognise the algebraic part of each term, carry signs correctly and simplify expressions with powers and mixed terms.
lessons.objective: Recognise the algebraic part of each term, carry signs correctly and simplify expressions with powers and mixed terms.
lessons.before: Read a term, its numerical coefficient and its variables. A term with no written coefficient has coefficient 1.
lessons.ideas:
Sort by the letters and their powers. Change only the coefficient when you combine a group.

\(xy=yx\), so those terms can combine. The terms \(x^2\) and \(x\) have different powers and stay separate.

Collect constants with constants. If a group’s coefficient adds to zero, leave that group out of the answer.
lessons.method:
Which terms can go together?

A term has a coefficient and an algebraic part. To decide what can be combined, compare the algebraic parts first.

What if the letters or powers look different?

Multiplication can be reordered within a term. Changing a power changes the term.

How do I handle constants and cancellation?

You can collect one group at a time and then write all the resulting non-zero terms together.
mistakes: \(5x+4y\) already has unlike terms. Combining the coefficient numbers would change the expression.
A term with two letters and a term with just one letter do not become like terms because they share one letter.
A pair such as \(8x^2-8x^2\) contributes zero. Its cancellation does not affect other terms.

examples.title: Collect terms with the same algebraic part
examples.question: Simplify \(4 x- 2 y- 12 x- 7 y\).
examples.solution:
Group matching algebraic parts, keeping the sign attached to each term.

\(4 x- 12 x- 2 y- 7 y\).

Combine the coefficient groups. \(\left(4-12\right)x+\left(-2-7\right)y=- 8 x - 9 y\).

examples.title: Collect terms with the same algebraic part
examples.question: Simplify \(26 x^{2}+24 x+11 x^{2}- 16 x\).
examples.solution:
Group matching algebraic parts, keeping the sign attached to each term.

\(26 x^{2}+11 x^{2}+24 x- 16 x\).

Combine the coefficient groups. \(\left(26+11\right)x^{2}+\left(24-16\right)x=37 x^{2} + 8 x\).

examples.title: Collect terms with the same algebraic part
examples.question: Simplify \(25 x^{2}+23 y-21- 25 x^{2}- 15 y\).
examples.solution:
Group matching algebraic parts, keeping the sign attached to each term.

\(25 x^{2}- 25 x^{2}+23 y- 15 y-21\).

Combine the coefficient groups. \(\left(25-25\right)x^{2}+\left(23-15\right)y+\left(-21\right)=8 y - 21\).

lessons.title: Expanding single brackets
lessons.summary: Distribute a signed number or monomial through one bracket, then collect any like terms that remain.
lessons.objective: Distribute a signed number or monomial through one bracket, then collect any like terms that remain.
lessons.before: Use signed multiplication and read adjacent factors as a product.
lessons.ideas:
\(a(b+c)=ab+ac\). Work through the terms one at a time.

Keep signed coefficients together. When the same letter is multiplied by itself, its powers add.

Expand each single bracket. A minus immediately before a bracket applies to the whole bracket.
lessons.method:
What does the outside factor multiply?

A rectangle with a common height can be split by width. The sum of the smaller areas is the full product.

What if the outside factor contains a sign or a letter?

For each product, decide the numerical sign first. Then multiply its letters.

How do I simplify after two separate expansions?

When expressions are added or subtracted, treat their outside factors as signed numbers or monomials.
mistakes: Multiplying only the first term changes the value and usually leaves the constant wrong.
For example, \((-3y)(-2y)=6y^2\). Two negative factors give a positive term.
A minus before the second bracket changes the sign of each term from that bracket.

examples.title: Distribute the outside factor
examples.question: Expand and simplify \(19\left(- 2 x+18\right)\).
examples.solution:
Multiply the outside factor by every term inside its bracket.

The products are \(- 38 x+342\).

The simplified result is \(342 - 38 x\).

examples.title: Distribute the outside factor
examples.question: Expand and simplify \(24 x\left(18 x- 17 y\right)\).
examples.solution:
Multiply the outside factor by every term inside its bracket.

The products are \(432 x^{2}- 408 x y\).

The simplified result is \(432 x^{2} - 408 x y\).

examples.title: Distribute the outside factor
examples.question: Expand and simplify \(17\left(23 x+16\right)-5\left(x-16\right)\).
examples.solution:
Expand each bracket separately. The sign before a bracket belongs to its outside factor.

Expand to \(391 x+272- 5 x+80\) before collecting like terms.

The simplified result is \(386 x + 352\).

lessons.title: Expanding two brackets in one variable
lessons.summary: Find all four products, combine the middle terms and explain what changes in a squared bracket.
lessons.objective: Find all four products, combine the middle terms and explain what changes in a squared bracket.
lessons.before: Expand a single bracket and identify like terms. In a two-bracket product make a row for each term of the first bracket.
lessons.ideas:
Each of two signed terms multiplies both signed terms in the other bracket. Record all four outcomes.

Rewrite the square as two identical factors. Both off-diagonal cells still contribute.

Two cross-products of the same magnitude and opposite sign add to zero. Only omit the middle term after checking that cancellation.
lessons.method:
How do I keep track of all four products?

A multiplication grid lets you see which two terms produced each cell.

How do I expand a squared bracket?

The two cross-products match when the brackets match, so add both of them.

When can the middle terms cancel?

Work out the two cross-products explicitly. They can reinforce or cancel each other.
mistakes: Starting with the two first terms and the two last terms misses the two cross-products.
\((x+4)^2\) has a middle term. Squaring the terms separately omits it.
Two opposite constant signs do not guarantee cancellation when the variable coefficients differ.

examples.title: Expand a product of two brackets
examples.question: Expand and simplify \(\left(x - 2\right)\left(x + 19\right)\).
examples.solution:
Place one bracket across the top and the other down the side. Multiply each row label by each column label.

×\(x\)\(19\)
\(x\)\(x^{2}\)\(19 x\)
\(-2\)\(- 2 x\)\(-38\)

Read all the cells and collect like terms. \(x^{2}+19 x- 2 x-38=x^{2} + 17 x - 38\).

examples.title: Expand a product of two brackets
examples.question: Expand and simplify \(\left(8 x + 24\right)\left(5 x - 18\right)\).
examples.solution:
Place one bracket across the top and the other down the side. Multiply each row label by each column label.

×\(5 x\)\(-18\)
\(8 x\)\(40 x^{2}\)\(- 144 x\)
\(24\)\(120 x\)\(-432\)

Read all the cells and collect like terms. \(40 x^{2}- 144 x+120 x-432=40 x^{2} - 24 x - 432\).

examples.title: Expand a product of two brackets
examples.question: Expand and simplify \(\left(7 x + 23\right)\left(7 x - 23\right)\).
examples.solution:
Place one bracket across the top and the other down the side. Multiply each row label by each column label.

×\(7 x\)\(-23\)
\(7 x\)\(49 x^{2}\)\(- 161 x\)
\(23\)\(161 x\)\(-529\)

Read all the cells and collect like terms. \(49 x^{2}- 161 x+161 x-529=49 x^{2} - 529\).

lessons.title: Factorising by a common factor
lessons.summary: Find the complete highest common monomial factor and check the remaining bracket by re-expansion.
lessons.objective: Find the complete highest common monomial factor and check the remaining bracket by re-expansion.
lessons.before: Find highest common factors of positive integers and multiply signed monomials.
lessons.ideas:
Use the highest common factor of the magnitudes of all coefficients. You may keep a positive coefficient outside.

A variable can go outside to the lowest power that appears in every term. If one term does not contain a letter, its shared power is zero.

Divide each term by the whole common factor and keep the original relative signs. The bracket should have no common factor left besides 1.
lessons.method:
How do I find the highest common number?

Factorising reverses distribution. The same factor must divide every term.

Which letters belong outside the bracket?

The highest common monomial combines a numerical factor and any shared powers of letters.

How do I tell whether the factorisation is complete?

Look at three-term expressions in exactly the same way. A factor must be present in all three terms.
mistakes: A factor that divides only the first coefficient is not shared.
An algebraic part can use more than one letter. Check each letter separately.
If a term equals the outside factor, its quotient is 1.

examples.title: Extract the whole common factor
examples.question: Factorise fully by extracting the highest common factor from \(76 x + 4\).
examples.solution:
Find what divides every coefficient and every term’s algebraic part. Here that gives \(4\).

Divide each term by \(4\) and put the quotients in one bracket.

\(76 x + 4=4\left(19 x + 1\right)\). Expand the product to check it.

examples.title: Extract the whole common factor
examples.question: Factorise fully by extracting the highest common factor from \(144 x^{2} + 8 x y\).
examples.solution:
Find what divides every coefficient and every term’s algebraic part. Here that gives \(8 x\).

Divide each term by \(8 x\) and put the quotients in one bracket.

\(144 x^{2} + 8 x y=8 x\left(18 x + y\right)\). Expand the product to check it.

examples.title: Extract the whole common factor
examples.question: Factorise fully by extracting the highest common factor from \(119 x^{2} + 14 x y + 7 x\).
examples.solution:
Find what divides every coefficient and every term’s algebraic part. Here that gives \(7 x\).

Divide each term by \(7 x\) and put the quotients in one bracket.

\(119 x^{2} + 14 x y + 7 x=7 x\left(17 x + 2 y + 1\right)\). Expand the product to check it.

lessons.title: Expanding multivariable and repeated products (Extended)
lessons.summary: Expand products with two letters and extend the multiplication method to three or more brackets.
lessons.objective: Expand products with two letters and extend the multiplication method to three or more brackets.
lessons.before: Expand two one-variable brackets and combine like powers.
lessons.ideas:
Multiply as usual. Combine the \(xy\) terms together and retain the \(x^2\) and \(y^2\) terms separately.

Multiply two brackets and simplify their product. Then multiply every term of that product by every term in the third bracket.

Treat a repeated bracket as another factor. Continue multiplying one unused factor at a time until no brackets remain.
lessons.method:
What changes if both brackets have two different letters?

The grid method still lists all four products. The letters tell you which terms are like.

How can I expand three brackets without losing terms?

You can choose any pair first. A convenient pair may have fewer terms in its expanded product.

What if a factor repeats or there are more than three?

Use the same distribution rule at every step. Repeated factors can be expanded early or left to the last step.
mistakes: \(x^2,xy,y^2\) are three different algebraic parts.
A quadratic result after the first multiplication is intermediate. One bracket is still unused.
The leading degree helps check for a missing factor. Four non-zero linear factors give degree four.

examples.title: Expand brackets containing two different letters
examples.question: Expand and simplify \(\left(2 x - 2 y\right)\left(6 x + 19 y\right)\).
examples.solution:
Place one bracket across the top and the other down the side. Multiply each row label by each column label.

×\(6 x\)\(19 y\)
\(2 x\)\(12 x^{2}\)\(38 x y\)
\(- 2 y\)\(- 12 x y\)\(- 38 y^{2}\)

Read all the cells and collect like terms. \(12 x^{2}+38 x y- 12 x y- 38 y^{2}=12 x^{2} + 26 x y - 38 y^{2}\).

examples.title: Expand three or more brackets in stages
examples.question: Expand and simplify \(\left(x + 24\right)\left(x - 18\right)\left(x + 17\right)\).
examples.solution:
Expand the first two brackets. \(\left(x + 24\right)\left(x - 18\right)=x^{2} + 6 x - 432\).

Multiply by the next unused bracket. \(\left(x^{2} + 6 x - 432\right)\left(x + 17\right)=x^{3} + 23 x^{2} - 330 x - 7344\).

examples.title: Expand three or more brackets in stages
examples.question: Expand and simplify \(\left(x + 23\right)\left(x + 23\right)\left(x + 17\right)\).
examples.solution:
Expand the first two brackets. \(\left(x + 23\right)\left(x + 23\right)=x^{2} + 46 x + 529\).

Multiply by the next unused bracket. \(\left(x^{2} + 46 x + 529\right)\left(x + 17\right)=x^{3} + 63 x^{2} + 1311 x + 8993\).

lessons.title: Factorising through grouping and identities (Extended)
lessons.summary: Recognise a shared bracket, a difference of two squares and a perfect square trinomial.
lessons.objective: Recognise a shared bracket, a difference of two squares and a perfect square trinomial.
lessons.before: Extract common monomial factors and multiply binomials with signs.
lessons.ideas:
Group two pairs. Extract a factor from each pair so an identical bracket appears twice. Then extract the whole bracket.

\(U^2-V^2=(U+V)(U-V)\). Check that both terms already are squares and that the sign between them is a minus.

\((U\pm V)^2=U^2\pm2UV+V^2\). The first and last squares alone are insufficient. Check the sign and size of the middle term.
lessons.method:
How can four terms hide a repeated bracket?

Recognise a repeated group as a factor, in the same way that a repeated letter can be a factor.

What tells me to use a difference of squares?

The two cross-products in the factorisation cancel. That is why the result contains only the two squares.

How can I recognise a square trinomial?

Both outer terms are squares. A negative middle term indicates a difference inside the bracket.
mistakes: Two brackets with opposite signs can become identical by taking an extra minus sign out of one group.
The rule uses one sum and one difference. Two identical factors usually create a non-zero middle term.
The middle term must be twice the product of the square roots.

examples.title: Factorise a repeated bracket
examples.question: Factorise fully by grouping \(2 x y- x+16 y-8\).
examples.solution:
Arrange the terms into two groups with the same bracket left inside.

\(x\left(2 y - 1\right)+8\left(2 y - 1\right)\).

Take out that common bracket as a single factor. \(\left(x + 8\right)\left(2 y - 1\right)\).

examples.title: Factorise a difference of two squares
examples.question: Factorise fully \(49 x^{2} - 625 y^{2}\).
examples.solution:
Identify the two squares \(\left(7 x\right)^2\) and \(\left(25 y\right)^2\).

Use \(U^2-V^2=(U+V)(U-V)\).

The factors are \(\left(7 x + 25 y\right)\left(7 x - 25 y\right)\).

examples.title: Spot a perfect square trinomial
examples.question: Factorise as a square \(81 x^{2} + 342 x y + 361 y^{2}\).
examples.solution:
The matching squares are \(\left(9 x\right)^2\) and \(\left(19 y\right)^2\).

The cross term must be twice the product. Here \(2\left(9 x\right)\left(19 y\right)=342 x y\).

So the factorised form is \(\left(9 x + 19 y\right)^2\).

lessons.title: Factorising quadratics and cubics with a common factor (Extended)
lessons.summary: Factorise monic and non-monic quadratics, then continue after extracting a common linear factor from a suitable cubic.
lessons.objective: Factorise monic and non-monic quadratics, then continue after extracting a common linear factor from a suitable cubic.
lessons.before: Expand binomial products and factorise pairs with a common bracket.
lessons.ideas:
Choose two numbers whose sum is the middle coefficient and whose product is the constant term.

Find two numbers whose sum is the middle coefficient and whose product is leading coefficient times constant. Split the middle term and regroup.

When every cubic term contains the variable, extract the highest common monomial factor. Then factorise the remaining quadratic if it can be split into linear factors over the integers. If no suitable split exists, leave that quadratic in one bracket.
lessons.method:
Which two constants build a monic quadratic?

A product of two monic linear factors has a cross-term equal to the sum of their constants times the variable.

What changes when the leading coefficient exceeds one?

The non-monic case still has two cross-products. Their product can be calculated before those cross-products are known.

How can a cubic become a quadratic factorisation?

These cubics have no constant term. In the form considered here, taking out the common variable leaves a quadratic.
mistakes: A pair that has the right product but the wrong sum changes the middle term.
Using only the constant term for the target product is the monic rule. Here the leading coefficient also matters.
Stopping at a linear factor times a factorable quadratic leaves the answer incomplete.

examples.title: Factorise a quadratic
examples.question: Factorise fully \(x^{2} + 17 x - 38\).
examples.solution:
Choose constants with product \(-38\) and sum \(17\). Those constants are \(-2\) and \(19\).

Write the complete product. \(\left(x - 2\right)\left(x + 19\right)\).

examples.title: Factorise a quadratic
examples.question: Factorise fully \(4 x^{2} + 77 x - 456\).
examples.solution:
Find the pair \(-19\) and \(96\). Their sum is \(77\) and their product is \(-1824\).

Split the middle term, then group. \(4 x^{2}- 19 x+96 x-456=x\left(4 x - 19\right)+24\left(4 x - 19\right)\).

Write the complete product. \(\left(x + 24\right)\left(4 x - 19\right)\).

examples.title: Factorise a cubic with an irreducible quadratic part
examples.question: Factorise fully \(35 x^{3} + 161 x^{2} + 196 x\).
examples.solution:
The greatest common monomial factor is \(7 x\).

Dividing each term by the factor leaves \(5 x^{2} + 23 x + 28\).

For the middle-term method the two numbers must have product \(140\) and sum \(23\). The possible sums with the right sign are \(141\), \(72\), \(39\), \(33\), \(27\), \(24\).

No integer middle-term split gives both the required sum and product for this bracket. The full factorisation is \(7 x\left(5 x^{2} + 23 x + 28\right)\).

lessons.title: Completing the square (Extended)
lessons.summary: Rewrite monic and non-monic quadratics in completed-square form, including fractional offsets and negative leading coefficients.
lessons.objective: Rewrite monic and non-monic quadratics in completed-square form, including fractional offsets and negative leading coefficients.
lessons.before: Expand two identical brackets and identify how the squared factor creates the linear term.
lessons.ideas:
The linear term in \((x+P)^2\) is \(2Px\). Take half of the coefficient to find \(P\), then subtract \(P^2\) to preserve the value.

Take the leading coefficient outside the quadratic and linear terms. Work out the half-coefficient inside, then multiply the constant correction by the factor outside.

A negative outside factor changes the signs of the coefficients when you divide the quadratic and linear terms to form the inside expression. Distribute the outside factor to the constant correction at the end.
lessons.method:
Why do I halve the linear coefficient?

The area model shows how two equal strips form the linear term and a corner completes the square when its width is positive.

How do I complete the square if the leading coefficient is not one?

A bracket with leading term \(x^2\) makes the monic method available even when the original coefficient is not one.

How do I handle a negative leading coefficient?

Work with the signed factor throughout. A fractional offset is still handled by taking exactly half of the inside coefficient.
mistakes: The added corner is the square of the half-coefficient, not the square of the whole coefficient.
The coefficient outside the brackets multiplies the correction as well as the squared expression.
The constant correction inside the bracket is negative, but multiplying it by a negative outside factor makes its contribution positive.

examples.title: Complete a quadratic expression to a square
examples.question: Complete the square for \(x^{2} + 38 x + 24\).
examples.solution:
The coefficient of \(x^2\) is already 1. Work on the quadratic and linear terms first.

These terms are \(x^{2} + 38 x\). The constant \(24\) stays outside the calculation of the square.

Half the coefficient of \(x\) inside the bracket is \(19\). Add and subtract \(361\) inside that bracket.

Multiply the constant correction by \(1\). \(x^{2} + 38 x + 24=\left(x + 19\right)^2-337\).

examples.title: Complete a quadratic expression to a square
examples.question: Complete the square for \(2 x^{2} - 72 x - 23\).
examples.solution:
Factor out the coefficient of \(x^2\) from the quadratic and linear terms.

\(2\left[x^{2} - 36 x\right]-23\).

Half the coefficient of \(x\) inside the bracket is \(-18\). Add and subtract \(324\) inside that bracket.

Multiply the constant correction by \(2\). \(2 x^{2} - 72 x - 23=2\left(x - 18\right)^2-671\).

examples.title: Complete a quadratic expression to a square
examples.question: Complete the square for \(- 7 x^{2} - 238 x + 22\).
examples.solution:
Factor out the coefficient of \(x^2\) from the quadratic and linear terms.

\(-7\left[x^{2} + 34 x\right]+22\).

Half the coefficient of \(x\) inside the bracket is \(17\). Add and subtract \(289\) inside that bracket.

Multiply the constant correction by \(-7\). \(- 7 x^{2} - 238 x + 22=-7\left(x + 17\right)^2+2045\).

questions.title: Collect terms with the same algebraic part
questions.prompt_html: Simplify \(18 x+16 y+3 x+21 y\). Enter the simplified coefficient for each listed group. Use 0 if a group cancels.

Group matching algebraic parts, keeping the sign attached to each term.

\(18 x+3 x+16 y+21 y\).

Combine the coefficient groups. \(\left(18+3\right)x+\left(16+21\right)y=21 x + 37 y\).

questions.prompt_html: Simplify \(- 17 x- 22 y- x-4+19 y+15 x\). Enter the simplified coefficient for each listed group. Use 0 if a group cancels.

Group matching algebraic parts, keeping the sign attached to each term.
